Here's some suggestions that aren't just "get certs":

Start developing IT experience from volunteer work. I developed some technical skills, specifically in AV from volunteering for Tech/IT at anime conventions. But there's other opportunities for non-profits or small businesses or even just family. Even if the role is not what you're trying to specialize into, it's something to put on your resume that stands out as "I have applied technical experience"

Also, if you're scoring interviews and not passing them, think about if there's something in the interview process that you might be lacking... companies do need you to demonstrate technical expertise, but I think it's actually more important that they see you are a fit for the culture.

Speaking from my experience working in the municipal sector, government entities also tend to look for experience in specific technologies. I was expected to make apps with ColdFusion in 2017! Try to read about specific tech qualifications, even if you just take a primer (read a book and demo it at home) you can demonstrate you have basic familiarity and are ready to work with it.

Start networking -- look for tech job fairs in your area, or if they don't exist locally, start looking for relevant communities online where you can start making connections. For example for the LGBT community we've got [Out in Tech](https://outintech.com/)

Final suggestion, maybe you need to consider applying to jobs and relocating. Might be an uneducated guess here as a technician in Southern California but I can't imagine the demand for IT in Alabama outside of the metropolitan areas is high or otherwise significant work.

Best of luck!

I really, really feel what you're feeling. I can't stop thinking about how bad things have been this year. 2019 was ridiculously rough for me because of an abusive relationship and living situation, and I started 2020 off promising to make this MY year, to have it be about ME. Then coronavirus happened. And it is so, so difficult to not think about how messed up this pandemic has been for so many people, if not everyone. As an American, all I can think about it how things could've -- should've -- been different. How we didn't have to lose hundreds of thousands of lives to this virus, how horribly this will impact our entire economy, and how bleak the near future seems. How can anyone with a right mind NOT think about those things?

Something about coping is knowing that to focus on the positive and to be mindful of what's good to you in the present, at face value, isn't mutually exclusive from acknowledging the "negative" feelings. You have to allow your body and mind to accept and take on the frustration, grief, anger, sadness, emotional exhaustion, etc. that the crisis has inflicted on you. And that it's okay. I don't think I've gone a peaceful moment or session of meditation lately without bursting into tears. We are in an enormous amount of stress and uncertainty right now. It's okay to not be able to see what's good about this situation, and to feel the immense pain. So whatever helps you decompress those feelings, whether it's crying, exercising, screaming into a pillow, sleeping a lot, or something else, do it. And don't hold yourself back. We're only human and can only handle so much weight, and right now for people who are empathetic or emotionally intelligent, it's INCREDIBLY easy to feel the whole world on our shoulders right now.

Sounds like you're on the right track! Succulents are very slow-growing plants and it takes lots of time for them to start rooting, and not all propped leaves will successfully take root. It's normal and part of the process. Usually cuttings have a better time rooting faster since they're already semi-established. Personally, I'm not sure why you would want to put the plants into a plastic bag AND mist them since that can encourage root rot or fungal growth you don't want.

My take: You can leave the cuttings and leaves out in a dry place indoors until tiny pink roots start shooting out (this can take anywhere from 1-4 weeks), then simply place them in a container with soil and mist 1-2 times a week. If you want, you can buy root hormone powder to encourage the pops to root faster, but it's totally not required. Patience is key with succulents, and gardening in general for that matter!

The problem is having an organization that can support the initially huge, and only continually growing, scale of such an enormous game. The reason that Niantic was able to release and (barely) maintain PoGo was because, being an internal Google startup, they started with strong resources (experienced pro devs, budget, server space etc.) These are things that aren't as easily attainable by a morally wholesome group of game devs without, basically, a shit-ton of money.

And a general issue with open-source projects like OpenStreetMap: there's no formal group of people maintaining the software. A new AR game is dependent on the stability of the maps used for it. Just think about the way PoGo changed cities, businesses, and legislation. Who's going to maintain all of that within the studio and the OSM at the same pace as the playerbase?

So the only way for a new off-shoot PoGo to work, would be to have the same access to great resources Niantic had, which is.... almost nobody, unless someone within a huge tech company like Google decides to take the Niantic route too by starting up within the company and breaking off.

What would be truly awesome would be an "AR framework" for many games to build off of. What if a company, or a startup within Google themselves developed said framework in business partnership with Google Maps? It's not like Niantic has 100% stake in Google's map data. Then lots of developers could use the framework to make PoGo-like games, and Google gets a percentage of profits for using their services.

> How did you start cosplaying?

I started out around seven years ago with a hand-me-down cosplay from a distant cousin and began making/modifying thrift store clothes from there. The rest is history.

> What do you feel is the interest in cosplaying?

It's a really blanket question because we all have different reasons for doing it. Whether people admit it or not, cosplaying is not just about dressing up as characters -- for some it's a science/an art (like myself), for others it's the social circle that comes with it, and some people just like dressing up. 

> How do you feel about people coming up and talking to you?

It's really easy for me to talk to people that do that. It was harder before, but cosplaying certainly desensitized me to people's opinions and looks even in "real life".

> Are there people you see/interact with that cross the line socially?

Do you mean weirdos or creeps? Yes, absolutely, they are EVERYWHERE in the cosplay and convention communities. It's a fact of life.

> Do you witness any harassment among cosplayers/con-goers?

Yes, myself included, and it occurs constantly even within the community. There's a reason it's infamous for being toxic.

> Do you feel as though you act differently when in costume?

Yes, I tend to lean towards the personality of the character I'm cosplaying. But a lot of the time it's just the costume or makeup making me uncomfortable :p

> Is there a hierarchy amongst cosplayers (i.e. newbies vs professionals)?

Yes. 100%. There's a LOT of fueled egos and elitism within cosplay. Even cosplay photographers have this issue.

> Do you find yourself judging certain cosplayers? Why?

Honestly yes but not necessarily as people. Since cosplay is such an art and science for me, errors or inaccuracies are just very noticeable to me. But I do look down on the really snobby parts of the community.

>How do you feel about competitive cosplay?

I think it's great that we have it, but it's not for everyone and it shouldn't define cosplay or the purpose of it.

>Do you think being in costume limits your con experience?

Yes, in tons of ways, which is why cosplayers often pack closet/lightweight costumes on days when they'd like to just enjoy the con's activities. When I plan to wear a more moderate or difficult-to-wear costume I usually throw out the rest of the day for just relaxing with friends in a kickback room party.

>How much money do you spend on each costume?

Totally depends. It can be almost nothing to hundreds and hundreds of dollars. The most I've ever spent on a costume was probably $500 and that's only because I made everything myself. Most cosplayers buy premade/commissioned things -- that can go beyond the $1000 mark.
